Parity denominator corrected from 82 to 80 (81 rules counted as (capability, BR id) pairs, minus the retired L1-posting/BR-009), per research/inputs/baseline-metrics.md and research/inputs/human-decisions.md. Baseline decisions now cite the human gate record .mw/runs/BASELINE-2026-10-30/baseline-review-report.json. outcome.statement: A Rust build of minidon (repository minidon-rust) that passes a parity test for every one of the 80 live baseline rules (81 rules minus the retired L1-posting/BR-009) and runs against existing minidon data without migration, ready for a separate cutover ticket.
outcome.problem: minidon runs on Python (FastAPI and SQLAlchemy on SQLite, 2,123 source lines, 6 capabilities, 81 business rules of which 80 are live, 40 HTTP endpoints). The team wants it on Rust. There is no Rust build yet: minidon-rust has no commits, so 0 of 80 rules are proven there. A rewrite risks silent behaviour changes and data incompatibility: 64 of the 81 rules were inferred from the code (DERIVED or mixed) rather than documented, the baseline needed 21 open questions and 7 doc-versus-code conflicts settled by a human at the baseline gate, Python and Rust differ in text-processing semantics (regex, length, case), and only about 50 of 81 rules cite an existing Python test.
affected: minidon maintainers and the delivery team
operators who run minidon against existing data

why.summary: The ticket asks to move minidon from Python to Rust as a lift and shift with feature parity on the same data, built from the confirmed baseline rather than translated line by line. The business reason for moving to Rust is not stated: the human decisions of 2026-11-12 record it as still open, for the PO to supply, and it stays a recorded risk (RISK-005). Performance parity is not requested. The value of this run is therefore proven parity, not a user-facing change.

valueHypothesis.for: minidon maintainers, the delivery team and current API clients
valueHypothesis.if: every baseline capability is rebuilt in Rust from specs derived from BASELINE-2026-10-30, each live rule gets a black-box parity test that passes against the Python reference first, and the Rust build uses the existing SQLite schema and storage formats
valueHypothesis.then: all 80 live baseline rules pass their parity test against the Rust build, all 6 capabilities are complete, and the Rust build reads and writes existing data with 0 migrations, so cutover can be planned as a separate ticket without re-discovering behaviour
valueHypothesis.falsifiedIf: By 2027-03-31: fewer than 80 of the 80 live baseline rules (81 (capability, BR id) pairs minus the retired L1-posting/BR-009) pass their parity test against the Rust build (MET-001), or running the Rust build on a Python-created database needs any schema or data migration (MET-004), or a differential run of the same request sequence (including non-ASCII text inputs) against both builds on copies of the same database shows a difference in status code or response body on any of the 40 endpoints that no baseline rule or agreed normalisation explains (which would show ASM-001 is wrong: the 80 live rules are not the whole behaviour).

metrics.name: Live baseline rules with a passing parity test against the Rust build

source.extractionMethod: git log on 2026-11-12: the repository is empty, so no rule can pass. Denominator 80 from research/inputs/baseline-metrics.md: 81 (capability, BR id) pairs across the six rules-trace files (accounts 14, following 15, posting 20, timelines 8, notifications 9, moderation 15), minus L1-posting/BR-009, retired at the baseline gate (CF-001)

measurement.method: Count of (capability, BR id) pairs, for example L1-accounts/BR-006, taken from the Rules Index and ### BR- sections of .mw/context/capabilities/*/rules-trace.md, excluding rules retired at the baseline gate (today only L1-posting/BR-009), whose parity test passes against both the Python reference and the Rust build in CI. A rule counts only if its test first passes against Python e1fbd3a. Bare BR ids are never counted, because ids restart in each capability.
measurement.cadence: every CI run on minidon-rust; reported weekly

metrics.name: Capabilities with every live baseline rule passing parity in Rust

measurement.method: Number of L1 capabilities for which every live rule passes its parity test: L1-accounts 14 of 14, L1-following 15 of 15, L1-posting 19 of 19 (BR-009 retired), L1-timelines 8 of 8, L1-notifications 9 of 9, L1-moderation 15 of 15

metrics.name: Existing Python test functions whose behaviour is covered by a passing black-box parity test

source.extractionMethod: empty repository; denominator 54 from research/inputs/baseline-metrics.md (def test_ count under tests/)

measurement.method: For each of the 54 def test_ functions in minidon/tests (6 files), a black-box parity test in minidon-rust covers the same behaviour and passes against both builds. The Python tests run in-process (tests/conftest.py overrides get_session with an in-memory database; tests/test_statuses.py:62-66 monkeypatches utcnow), which a black-box harness cannot do. So the equivalent is not a one-to-one translation: clock-dependent tests are re-expressed with controlled data timestamps in a shared database file (RISK-008, NFR-005). Any test that cannot be expressed black-box is listed in the traceability matrix with the reason and does not count. Mapping kept in the traceability matrix from planning.

metrics.name: Schema or data migrations needed for Rust to run on existing minidon data

source.extractionMethod: The Python build creates its schema with Base.metadata.create_all and has no migration tool, so today's data needs 0 migrations to run on today's code

measurement.method: Compatibility suite: start the Rust build on a copy of a Python-created SQLite database and run the parity suite; then let Python read data written by Rust. Count any schema change, data rewrite or manual step required.

metrics.name: Changes to the Python minidon repository since the baseline commit

source.extractionMethod: git log and git status on 2026-11-12: HEAD is still the baseline commit e1fbd3a and the working tree is clean

measurement.method: git rev-list --all --count ^e1fbd3a on the minidon repository (every commit on any branch or tag that is not in the baseline commit, whatever its message), plus the number of entries in git status --porcelain (uncommitted or untracked changes). No filter on ticket references.

in: Reimplement all 6 baseline capabilities (L1-accounts, L1-following, L1-posting, L1-timelines, L1-notifications, L1-moderation) in Rust in the new repository minidon-rust
The same external behaviour for all 80 live baseline rules and the 40 HTTP endpoints: same request, same status code and response body

The shared platform behaviour with observable effects: app wiring, DomainError to HTTP status mapping (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422, 429), the two 422 body shapes, authentication dependencies, configuration (MINIDON_DATABASE_URL, MINIDON_DOMAIN and the Settings defaults)
Text-processing parity with Python: mention and hashtag regex, length limits counted in code points, Unicode case folding and trimming (NFR-010)
Reading and writing the existing SQLite schema and storage formats, including existing PBKDF2 password hashes and access tokens, with no migration
A parity test suite that runs every test against the Python reference and the Rust build

The cross-capability decisions from the baseline gate: L1-accounts owns get_by_username as a stable identity API (CF-004); Moderation calls Posting's soft delete directly and the boost cascade is intended (CF-006); the social queries module stays a plain import owned by L1-following (CF-003)
out: Cutover, parallel running and retirement of the Python version (separate ticket)
Any change to the Python minidon repository
Porting the dead Lists code (minidon/lists/); the gate decided to delete it as a follow-up (CF-002, OQ-020, OQ-021)
Gate follow-up: secure admin seeding by env or CLI, replacing first-registrant-becomes-Admin (OQ-001, instance takeover risk)
Gate follow-up: raise the minimum password length from 8 to 12 (OQ-002)
Gate follow-up: raise password hashing to OWASP level (600,000 PBKDF2-SHA256) or argon2id, with rehash on login (OQ-003)
Gate follow-up: an audit trail for staff deletes (OQ-009)
Gate follow-up: a test guard for new notification kinds (OQ-012)
Gate follow-up: README updates (OQ-010, OQ-015, CF-007) and repair or supersession of ADR-001 and the 2026-10-01 decision record to 60 minutes (CF-001)
Gate follow-up: document the get_by_username identity contract (CF-004) and the boost cascade in L1-moderation/BR-015 (CF-006)
Gate follow-up: delete the dead minidon/lists/ code in the Python repository (CF-002)
nonGoals: New features or behaviour changes, including fixes for known weaknesses
Performance improvement or performance parity (not requested; nothing is measured)
A line-by-line translation of the Python code
Renaming domain terms: the gate adopted Relationship as the official business term (OQ-006), which the Rust build uses as is

guardrails.rule: The Rust build uses the existing SQLite schema and storage formats unchanged: no migration, no new tables, no column or format change

Every live baseline rule has a parity test, and each parity test must pass against the Python reference before it counts for the Rust build. Rules retired at the baseline gate (L1-posting/BR-009) get no parity test

source.extractionMethod: The ticket states the parity test; the Python-first rule is inferred from 'serves as the reference'; the retirement of BR-009 is STATED in the baseline gate record CF-001

guardrails.rule: Build from the baseline specs, not by translating the Python code line by line; the Python code is consulted only to settle what a rule means

Existing PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 hashes ('<salt hex>$<digest hex>', 100,000 iterations) and existing access tokens keep working; password comparison stays constant time; hashing parameters do not change in this rebuild (raising them is a gate follow-up, out of scope)

source.location: OQ-003 gate answer (kurtis, 2026-11-10: known gap, raise as follow-up); human-decisions ## 3 (follow-ups out of scope). Hash format and iteration count read from minidon/accounts/service.py:21-35 at e1fbd3a

guardrails.rule: Where documentation and code disagree, the Rust build copies the code: edit window 60 minutes (L1-posting/BR-010; BR-009 retired), boost only public and unlisted (L1-posting/BR-016)
The Python minidon repository is never written to by this run

The Rust build reads the same configuration as Python (MINIDON_DATABASE_URL defaulting to sqlite:///./minidon.db, MINIDON_DOMAIN defaulting to minidon.local) with the same Settings defaults, and its development entry point listens on 127.0.0.1:8000 like python -m minidon
Time-dependent rules are tested with a controlled clock or controlled data timestamps, never with real waits

Text handling matches Python exactly, including non-ASCII input: the mention and hashtag patterns (with their lookbehinds and Unicode \w and \b), length limits counted in code points, Unicode lower-casing and whitespace trimming. Unicode inputs are a required class in the parity suite
